source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: A client with acute kidney injury has decreased erythropoietin production. Upon analysis of the client’s complete blood count, the nurse will expect which of the following results?
options: An increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and red cell distribution width (RDW)
A decreased mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and red cell distribution width (RDW)
An increased hemoglobin and decreased hematocrit
rationale: Erythropoietin from the kidneys stimulates red blood cell production. When acute kidney injury reduces erythropoietin, fewer erythrocytes are produced, so hemoglobin and hematocrit decrease; MCV and RDW describe red cell size and variation, not the primary expected result.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: What is hematopoiesis?
options: The production of lymphatic fluid in the body
The making of red blood cells and lymph
The manufacture and development of blood cells
The development of lymph in the bone marrow
correctAnswers: The manufacture and development of blood cells
rationale: Hematopoiesis means the formation and maturation of blood cells in the bone marrow. It includes red cells, white cells, and platelets, so answers limited to lymph fluid or lymph development are too narrow.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's white blood cell count with the client. As part of the discussion, the nurse explains about granulocytes and agranulocytes and their function. Which type of white blood cell would the nurse describe as being most numerous?
rationale: Neutrophils are the most abundant circulating white blood cells and are major early responders in acute inflammation and bacterial infection. Basophils and eosinophils are much less numerous, and T cells are lymphocytes rather than the most common granulocyte.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: Which type of leukocyte contains histamine and is an important part of hypersensitivity reactions?
rationale: Basophils contain histamine-containing granules and contribute to allergic and hypersensitivity reactions. Neutrophils mainly perform phagocytosis, erythrocytes carry oxygen, and B lymphocytes are associated with antibody-mediated immunity.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: A client is seeing the health care provider at the clinic and tells the nurse they are fatigued and short of breath with minimal exertion. What lab study best reflects a decrease in transport of oxygen?
rationale: Erythrocytes carry hemoglobin, which transports oxygen to tissues. A low erythrocyte count directly reduces oxygen-carrying capacity and explains fatigue and dyspnea; leukocytes reflect immune activity, platelets reflect clotting, and albumin reflects protein/nutritional status.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: Which of the following is the most common hematologic condition affecting older adults
rationale: Anemia is the most common hematologic problem in older adults and is often reflected by reduced hemoglobin or hematocrit. Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia can occur, but they are not the most common broad hematologic condition in this group.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: A client with a diagnosis of pernicious anemia comes to the clinic and reports numbness and tingling in the arms and legs. What do these symptoms indicate?
options: Loss of vibratory and position senses
rationale: Pernicious anemia is related to vitamin B12 deficiency, and B12 deficiency can injure neurologic pathways. Numbness and tingling therefore point to neurologic involvement rather than simply inadequate iron intake or a nonspecific marker of severity.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: Which cells are also known as platelets?
rationale: Platelets are also called thrombocytes and are central to primary hemostasis and clot formation. Erythrocytes are red blood cells, basophils are leukocytes, and plasma is the liquid portion of blood.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: The nurse is collecting data for a client who has been diagnosed with iron-deficiency anemia. What subjective findings does the nurse recognize as symptoms related to this type of anemia?
options: “I have a difficult time falling asleep at night.”
“I have difficulty breathing when walking 30 feet.”
“I have an increase in my appetite.”
“I feel hot all of the time.”
correctAnswers: “I have difficulty breathing when walking 30 feet.”
rationale: Iron-deficiency anemia reduces hemoglobin formation and therefore oxygen delivery. Dyspnea with mild exertion fits decreased oxygen-carrying capacity; increased appetite, feeling hot, or insomnia are not the classic subjective findings for this anemia.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-01-hematology-blood-cells.md
stem: While monitoring a client for the development of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), the nurse should take note of which assessment parameters?
options: Thrombin time, calcium levels, and potassium levels
Platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time
Platelet count, blood glucose levels, and white blood cell (WBC) count
Fibrinogen level, WBC, and platelet count
correctAnswers: Platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time
rationale: DIC consumes platelets and clotting factors while widespread clotting and bleeding occur. Platelet count, PT, and PTT are central monitoring values because they show thrombocytopenia and prolonged coagulation times; glucose, calcium, and potassium do not track the coagulopathy directly.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: A client reports having 1 bowel movement per week; this is considered constipation.
rationale: One bowel movement per week is below the usual expected range and is consistent with constipation. Constipation is judged by infrequent stools, difficulty passing stool, or hard stools, not only by complete absence of bowel movements.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: Diarrhea is always the results of a bacterial or viral infection.
rationale: Diarrhea can be caused by infection, but it can also result from medications, inflammation, malabsorption, diet, or other GI disorders. Because infection is not the only cause, the statement is false.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: A client has a gastrointestinal (GI) disorder that affects absorption of nutrients. Which layer of the gastrointestinal system would the nurse suspect is malfunctioning in this client?
rationale: The mucosal layer is the absorptive and secretory lining of the GI tract. If nutrient absorption is impaired, the mucosa is the layer most directly involved; the muscularis moves contents and the serosa is the outer protective layer.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: Causes of peptic ulcers include which of the following? (Select all that apply)
rationale: Peptic ulcer disease is strongly associated with H. pylori infection, NSAID-related mucosal injury, and high-acid states such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Constipation, hypertension, and allergies are not primary ulcer mechanisms.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: What begins the digestive process?
rationale: Digestion begins in the mouth, where saliva moistens food and enzymes such as amylase begin chemical breakdown. The stomach and small intestine continue digestion later, but they do not begin the process.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: The gastrointestinal system is sterile.
rationale: The GI tract is not sterile; it normally contains large numbers of microorganisms, especially in the colon. Normal flora contribute to digestion, vitamin production, and immune interactions, so the statement is false.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: Risk factors for constipation include which of the following? (Select all that apply)
rationale: The correct choices are the options that are directly supported by the clinical concept in the stem. Eliminate options that describe a different disease process, drug effect, or assessment priority even if they sound generally related.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: The physiology instructor is discussing the GI system with the pre-nursing class. What should the instructor tell the students is a function of the GI tract?
options: The reabsorption of medication not needed by the body
The elimination of digested unabsorbed vegetable matter and other waste products
The absorption into the bloodstream of small nutrient molecules produced by digestion
The breakdown of food particles into the atomic form for digestion
correctAnswers: The absorption into the bloodstream of small nutrient molecules produced by digestion
rationale: A core GI function is absorbing small nutrient molecules produced by digestion into the bloodstream. The GI tract also eliminates waste, but the best answer here is nutrient absorption rather than reabsorbing medication or breaking food into individual atoms.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: Endoscopy of a 56-year-old client has revealed the presence of a duodenal ulcer. The nurse who is providing this client's care is assessing for risk factors that may have contributed to the development of this disease. What question most directly addresses these risk factors?
options: “Have you felt extra emotional stress recently?”
“Do you ever find it difficult to swallow certain foods?”
rationale: Smoking is a recognized risk factor that can impair mucosal defenses and delay ulcer healing. Stress and anxiety may affect symptoms, and dysphagia suggests another problem, but smoking most directly addresses ulcer risk in the options.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-02-gastrointestinal-foundations.md
stem: What is the removal of possibly toxic substances triggered by the medulla called?
rationale: Vomiting is coordinated by centers in the medulla and helps expel potentially harmful gastric contents. Elimination is broader waste removal, swallowing moves material into the GI tract, and peristalsis propels contents forward.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: Short acting muscarinic antagonist and long acting muscarinic antagonist are medications that can be used by themselves in an acute airway emergency.
rationale: Short- and long-acting muscarinic antagonists can help bronchodilation, but they are not used by themselves as the rescue treatment in an acute airway emergency. Acute bronchospasm requires rapid rescue therapy such as a SABA and appropriate emergency assessment/support.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A client is admitted in acute renal failure and prescribed mannitol. The nurse prepares to administer this drug via which route?
rationale: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that is administered intravenously. It is not given orally, subcutaneously, or intramuscularly for acute renal failure because the intended osmotic effect requires IV delivery.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: The nurse is providing education to a client with asthma on the therapeutic action of inhaled corticosteroid agents. How will the nurse describe the action?
options: Inhaled corticosteroid agents will depress the central nervous system.
Inhaled corticosteroid agents reduce airway inflammation.
Inhaled corticosteroid agents reduce respiratory rate.
correctAnswers: Inhaled corticosteroid agents reduce airway inflammation.
rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation and help prevent asthma exacerbations over time. They are controller medications, not rescue bronchodilators, so they do not provide the rapid relief expected from albuterol.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: The nurse is assessing the client for left-sided heart failure. Which symptom would the nurse identify as left-ventricular heart failure? (Select all that apply.)
rationale: Left-sided heart failure backs blood into the pulmonary circulation and also reduces forward cardiac output. Cough and dyspnea reflect pulmonary congestion, and tachycardia is a compensatory response; neck vein distention and hepatic engorgement fit right-sided systemic venous congestion better.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: What is the difference between respiration and ventilation?
options: Ventilation is the movement of air in and out of the respiratory tract.
Ventilation is the process of getting oxygen to the cells.
Ventilation is the exchange of gases in the lung.
Ventilation is the process of gas exchange.
correctAnswers: Ventilation is the movement of air in and out of the respiratory tract.
rationale: Ventilation is the mechanical movement of air into and out of the respiratory tract. Respiration refers more broadly to gas exchange and oxygen use, so choices describing gas exchange are not the best definition of ventilation.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a history of high blood pressure and heart failure. The client has been prescribed hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) 12.5 mg daily. What action(s) should the nurse take before administering this medication? Select all that apply.
options: Ensure the client's potassium level is within normal limits.
Instruct the client to eat a diet low in sodium and potassium.
Encourage taking additional fluids to assist with absorption.
correctAnswers: Ensure the client's potassium level is within normal limits.
rationale: Hydrochlorothiazide can lower blood pressure and alter electrolytes, especially potassium, and it has a sulfonamide-related allergy consideration. Before giving it, checking vital signs, sulfonamide allergy history, and potassium is safer than encouraging extra fluids or a low-potassium diet.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: When planning a client's treatment regimen for administration of medication, which factors must be considered for inclusion in the teaching plan? (Select all that apply.)
options: Method used to administer the drug
Type of reaction to expect from the drug
To call the health care provider after the first week
Information to report to the health care provider
correctAnswers: Method used to administer the drug
Type of reaction to expect from the drug
Information to report to the health care provider
rationale: Teaching should cover how the drug is given, what therapeutic or adverse reactions to expect, and what findings should be reported to the provider. Dose calculation is a nursing responsibility, and a blanket instruction to call after the first week is less useful than teaching specific reportable problems.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A patient receiving norepinephrine suddenly reports burning and pain at the IV site, and the area appears pale and cool. What is the nurse’s first priority action?
options: Stop the infusion immediately (do not remove the IV).
Apply a warm compress to the IV site.
Administer phentolamine (an alpha-adrenergic blocker) if ordered to counteract local vasoconstriction.
Remove the IV catheter and start a new line in the opposite arm.
correctAnswers: Stop the infusion immediately (do not remove the IV).
rationale: Burning, pain, pallor, and coolness at a norepinephrine IV site suggest extravasation with intense local vasoconstriction. The priority is to stop the infusion while leaving the IV in place for possible antidote administration, then follow protocol and notify the provider.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: Which is a characteristic clinical manifestation of acute kidney injury?
rationale: Acute kidney injury reduces renal filtration, so nitrogenous wastes such as BUN rise. Decreased BUN or creatinine would not fit impaired filtration, and urine specific gravity changes depend on the cause and stage.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A client admitted with acute anxiety has the following arterial blood gas (ABG) values: pH, 7.55; partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2), 90 mm Hg; partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2), 27 mm Hg; and bicarbonate (HCO3–), 24 mEq/L. Based on these values, the nurse suspects:
rationale: The pH is alkalotic and the PaCO2 is low, which points to excessive ventilation blowing off carbon dioxide. The bicarbonate is normal, so the primary disorder is respiratory alkalosis rather than a metabolic imbalance.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: Match the clinical effect of epinephrine to its mechanism:
correctAnswers: Increased heart rate and contractility -> Beta 1 receptor stimulation
Vasoconstriction and increased BP -> Alpha receptor stimulation
rationale: Epinephrine stimulates different adrenergic receptors in different tissues: beta-1 increases heart rate and contractility, alpha receptors cause vasoconstriction and pupil dilation, and beta-2 causes bronchodilation. Matching the effect to the receptor is the key pharmacodynamic concept.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of symptomatic hypomagnesemia in the United States?
rationale: Alcohol use disorder is the most common cause of symptomatic hypomagnesemia in the United States because poor intake, GI loss, and renal magnesium wasting can occur together. The other options can affect magnesium but are not the most common cause emphasized here.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A nurse is caring for a 73-year-old female client who just arrived to the medical surgical floor following a radical mastectomy for breast cancer. The nurse will encourage the client to cough and deep breathe to help prevent:
rationale: Coughing, deep breathing, and incentive spirometry expand alveoli and help prevent postoperative alveolar collapse, which is atelectasis. These actions do not primarily prevent bleeding, sinusitis, or asthma.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: The nurse has been closely monitoring the blood work of a client who recently experienced nephrotoxic effects from an over-the-counter medication. In the course of providing care, the nurse has been teaching the client about the various roles that the kidney plays in the maintenance of homeostasis. Which of the following functions is performed by the kidneys?
rationale: The kidneys help maintain homeostasis by regulating acid-base balance through hydrogen ion secretion and bicarbonate handling. They also affect fluid, electrolytes, blood pressure, and erythropoietin, but they do not primarily regulate digestion or protein synthesis.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A nurse is assessing a client who comes to the clinic for care. Which findings in this client suggest bacterial pneumonia?
rationale: The saved course quiz keyed dyspnea and wheezing for findings suggesting bacterial pneumonia. Clinically, pneumonia often also includes fever, productive cough, crackles, or abnormal oxygenation; the other listed options pair symptoms that are less consistent with pneumonia.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A group of students are reviewing the mechanics of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange in the alveoli. The students demonstrate understanding when they identify which mechanism as being responsible?
rationale: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move across the alveolar-capillary membrane by diffusion down their partial-pressure gradients. Active transport, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion are not the primary mechanisms for alveolar gas exchange.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A client is prescribed a leukotriene receptor antagonist. The nurse should evaluate the effectiveness of the medication therapy based on the long term management of symptoms associated with which respiratory condition?
rationale: Leukotriene receptor antagonists are controller medications used for long-term asthma symptom management by reducing leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction and inflammation. They are not rescue drugs and are not primarily used for pneumonia, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: The volume of air inhaled and exhaled with each breath is termed:
rationale: Tidal volume is the amount of air inhaled and exhaled with each normal breath. Vital capacity, residual volume, and expiratory reserve volume describe different lung-volume measurements.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A junior-level nursing class has just finished learning about the management of clients with chronic pulmonary diseases. Which of the following disorders is classified as COPD?
rationale: Emphysema is one of the classic chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases. Asthma is usually treated as a reversible obstructive disease, while cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis are different chronic pulmonary disorders.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: The nurse is assessing a client who, after an extensive surgical procedure, is at risk for developing acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). The nurse assesses for which most common early sign of ARDS?
rationale: An early prominent sign of ARDS is the rapid onset of severe dyspnea with worsening oxygenation after a major insult. Crackles or cyanosis can occur, but rapid severe dyspnea is the most useful early warning sign among these options.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: Decrease mental function in an older adult may seem like a normal part of aging, but it can result from disease or another cause. What should the ER staff do first for a presenting older adult with a mental dysfunction such as extreme confusion?
rationale: New confusion in an older adult can be caused or worsened by medications, interactions, or adverse drug effects. Reviewing the current drug list is a high-priority first step before assuming the change is normal aging or immediately giving additional medication.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: Which symptoms would likely be present in a client with right-ventricular heart failure? (Select all that apply)
rationale: Right-sided heart failure causes systemic venous congestion, leading to peripheral edema, neck vein distention, hepatic congestion, and nocturia. Orthopnea, crackles, and frothy sputum are more typical of left-sided pulmonary congestion.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: Before administering a prescribed bronchodilator to a client experiencing acute breathing distress, which assessment(s) should the nurse complete? Select all that apply.
rationale: Before a bronchodilator in acute distress, the nurse should assess respiratory status and cardiovascular tolerance: respiratory rate, lung sounds, pulse, and blood pressure. Blood glucose is not a routine immediate pre-administration assessment for most bronchodilators.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: A client has been prescribed a first-generation antihistamine. What adverse effects should the nurse describe during client teaching? Select all that apply.
rationale: Diphenhydramine has anticholinergic effects, which commonly include dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention. It does not typically cause excessive salivation, diarrhea, or pupillary constriction.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem: After reviewing information about drugs used to treat lower respiratory system conditions, a group of nursing students demonstrate understanding of the information when they identify which as an example of a short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA)?
rationale: Albuterol is the best answer because it directly addresses the mechanism, assessment finding, or safety priority described in the stem. The distractors are less appropriate because they apply to a different condition, drug effect, or nursing action.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-03-mixed-pharm-resp-cardiac-renal-case.md
stem:
Case Study: Renal
ES is a 65-year-old cisgender female who is being seen in the office today reporting persistent fatigue, lower extremity swelling, that she is urinating less and that she is having occasional shortness of breath.
Medical History: Long-standing diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, hyperlipidemia
Physical Examination: 
Appearance: Appears fatigued and pale. In no apparent distress. 
Vital Signs: 144/88, 96, 18, 36.9º, 98% on RA 
Edema: 2+ pitting edema in both lower extremities.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal but within her records there is evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy on an echocardiogram from earlier this year.
Diagnosis: Mrs. S was diagnosed today in clinic with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3b, primarily due to her diabetes and hypertension.  
Her current medication anagement:
Lisinopril
Metformin
Atorvastatin

You are reviewing the new medication that have been prescribed for E.S. You question the health care provider's prescription for oral spironolactone because the client's health problems would contribute to a high risk of which adverse reaction?
rationale: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing, and chronic kidney disease reduces potassium excretion. Together, especially with diabetes, hypertension, or ACE inhibitor therapy, they make hyperkalemia the adverse reaction of greatest concern.

As you are providing medication teaching to Mrs. S, she asks you why having diabetes and high blood pressure causes problems for her kidneys.  You respond:
options: These diseases mainly affect only the bladder, not the kidneys.
They cause dehydration, which strengthens kidney tissue.
These conditions cause increased blood flow and oxygen to the kidneys, improving filtration.
Elevated blood sugar and high pressure damage kidney blood vessels and filtering units (nephrons).
correctAnswers: Elevated blood sugar and high pressure damage kidney blood vessels and filtering units (nephrons).
rationale: Elevated blood glucose and sustained high pressure damage renal blood vessels and nephron filtering structures over time. This chronic microvascular injury reduces filtration and leads to CKD; the problem is not limited to the bladder and does not strengthen kidney tissue.

stem:
Case Study: Renal
ES is a 65-year-old cisgender female who is being seen in the office today reporting persistent fatigue, lower extremity swelling, that she is urinating less and that she is having occasional shortness of breath.
Medical History: Long-standing diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, hyperlipidemia
Physical Examination: 
Appearance: Appears fatigued and pale. In no apparent distress. 
Vital Signs: 144/88, 96, 18, 36.9º, 98% on RA 
Edema: 2+ pitting edema in both lower extremities.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal but within her records there is evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy on an echocardiogram from earlier this year.
Diagnosis: Mrs. S was diagnosed today in clinic with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3b, primarily due to her diabetes and hypertension.  
Her current medication anagement:
Lisinopril
Metformin
Atorvastatin

The provider asked E.S. to return to the clinic in two weeks for follow-up. Laboratory tests were ordered. At the follow-up visit, you reviewed the results. You determine they are at risk for electrolyte imbalance based on which result(s)? Select all that apply.
rationale: Sodium 124 mEq/L is hyponatremia and potassium 2.9 mEq/L is hypokalemia, so both represent clinically important electrolyte imbalance. Sodium 139, potassium 4.5, and magnesium 2 are within typical reference ranges.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: A client admitted with acute anxiety has the following arterial blood gas (ABG) values: pH, 7.55; partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2), 90 mm Hg; partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2), 27 mm Hg; and bicarbonate (HCO3–), 24 mEq/L. Based on these values, the nurse suspects:
rationale: The pH is alkalotic and the PaCO2 is low, which points to excessive ventilation blowing off carbon dioxide. The bicarbonate is normal, so the primary disorder is respiratory alkalosis rather than a metabolic imbalance.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: The nurse has been closely monitoring the blood work of a client who recently experienced nephrotoxic effects from an over-the-counter medication. In the course of providing care, the nurse has been teaching the client about the various roles that the kidney plays in the maintenance of homeostasis. Which of the following functions is performed by the kidneys?
rationale: The kidneys help maintain homeostasis by regulating acid-base balance through hydrogen ion secretion and bicarbonate handling. They also affect fluid, electrolytes, blood pressure, and erythropoietin, but they do not primarily regulate digestion or protein synthesis.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: A nurse is caring for a client with metastatic breast cancer who is extremely lethargic and very slow to respond to stimuli. The laboratory report indicates a serum calcium level of 12.0 mg/dl, a serum potassium level of 3.9 mEq/L, a serum chloride level of 101 mEq/L, and a serum sodium level of 140 mEq/L. Based on this information, the nurse determines that the client's symptoms are most likely associated with which electrolyte imbalance?
rationale: A calcium level of 12.0 mg/dL is elevated and can cause lethargy, slowed responses, weakness, and other neurologic changes. The potassium, chloride, and sodium values given are not the abnormal values driving the symptoms.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: A nurse is providing client teaching about the body's plasma pH and the client asks the nurse what is the major chemical regulator of plasma pH. What is the best response by the nurse?
rationale: The bicarbonate-carbonic acid buffer system is the major chemical buffer for plasma pH. It works with the lungs and kidneys to regulate carbon dioxide and bicarbonate, making it more directly relevant than RAAS or hormone systems.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: End stage kidney disease (stage 5) is defined as GFR <15 mL/min.
rationale: Stage 5 kidney disease is defined by a severely reduced GFR, typically less than 15 mL/min. That threshold indicates kidney failure-level loss of filtration, so the statement is true.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: Which of the following are risk factors for chronic kidney disease? (Select all that apply)
rationale: Hypertension and diabetes mellitus are major risk factors for chronic kidney disease because they chronically injure renal vasculature and nephrons. Exercise and a low-sodium diet are generally protective rather than risk factors.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: Which is a characteristic clinical manifestation of acute kidney injury?
rationale: Acute kidney injury reduces renal filtration, so nitrogenous wastes such as BUN rise. Decreased BUN or creatinine would not fit impaired filtration, and urine specific gravity changes depend on the cause and stage.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of symptomatic hypomagnesemia in the United States?
rationale: Alcohol use disorder is the most common cause of symptomatic hypomagnesemia in the United States because poor intake, GI loss, and renal magnesium wasting can occur together. The other options can affect magnesium but are not the most common cause emphasized here.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: The nurse is instructing a health class of high school seniors on the function of the kidney. The nurse is correct to highlight which information? (Select all that apply)
options: Regulates calcium and the synthesis of vitamin D
correctAnswers: Regulates calcium and the synthesis of vitamin D
rationale: Kidneys excrete waste products, regulate fluid/electrolytes and acid-base balance, help control blood pressure, activate vitamin D/calcium balance, and produce erythropoietin for red blood cell production. They do not regulate estrogen/progesterone or produce surfactant.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-04-renal-electrolytes-acid-base.md
stem: The majority of acute kidney injuries are the result of pre-renal failure (e.g. volume depletion, decreased cardiac output, vasodilation).
rationale: Most acute kidney injuries are prerenal, commonly from decreased renal perfusion due to volume depletion, reduced cardiac output, or vasodilation. The kidney tissue may initially be structurally intact, but filtration falls because blood flow is inadequate.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: A nurse is assessing a client who comes to the clinic for care. Which findings in this client suggest bacterial pneumonia?
rationale: The saved course quiz keyed dyspnea and wheezing for findings suggesting bacterial pneumonia. Clinically, pneumonia often also includes fever, productive cough, crackles, or abnormal oxygenation; the other listed options pair symptoms that are less consistent with pneumonia.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: The nurse is assessing a client who, after an extensive surgical procedure, is at risk for developing acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). The nurse assesses for which most common early sign of ARDS?
rationale: An early prominent sign of ARDS is the rapid onset of severe dyspnea with worsening oxygenation after a major insult. Crackles or cyanosis can occur, but rapid severe dyspnea is the most useful early warning sign among these options.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: A junior-level nursing class has just finished learning about the management of clients with chronic pulmonary diseases. Which of the following disorders is classified as COPD?
rationale: Emphysema is one of the classic chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases. Asthma is usually treated as a reversible obstructive disease, while cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis are different chronic pulmonary disorders.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: What is the difference between respiration and ventilation?
options: Ventilation is the process of getting oxygen to the cells.
Ventilation is the movement of air in and out of the respiratory tract.
Ventilation is the exchange of gases in the lung.
Ventilation is the process of gas exchange.
correctAnswers: Ventilation is the movement of air in and out of the respiratory tract.
rationale: Ventilation is the mechanical movement of air into and out of the respiratory tract. Respiration refers more broadly to gas exchange and oxygen use, so choices describing gas exchange are not the best definition of ventilation.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: What allows the alveoli sac to stay open and allows for exchange of gases?
rationale: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move across the alveolar-capillary membrane by diffusion down their partial-pressure gradients. Active transport, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion are not the primary mechanisms for alveolar gas exchange.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: The nurse assessed a 28-year-old client who was experiencing dyspnea severe enough to make them seek medical attention. The history revealed no prior cardiac problems and the presence of symptoms for 6 months' duration. On assessment, the nurse noted the presence of both inspiratory and expiratory wheezing. Based on this data, which of the following diagnoses is likely?
rationale: A several-month history of dyspnea with both inspiratory and expiratory wheezing and no prior cardiac problem fits asthma. Pneumothorax and acute obstruction are usually more abrupt, while ARDS is a severe acute inflammatory lung injury.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: A group of students are reviewing the mechanics of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange in the alveoli. The students demonstrate understanding when they identify which mechanism as being responsible?
rationale: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move across the alveolar-capillary membrane by diffusion down their partial-pressure gradients. Active transport, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion are not the primary mechanisms for alveolar gas exchange.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: A nurse is caring for a 73-year-old female client who just arrived to the medical surgical floor following a radical mastectomy for breast cancer. The nurse will encourage the client to cough and deep breathe to help prevent:
rationale: Coughing, deep breathing, and incentive spirometry expand alveoli and help prevent postoperative alveolar collapse, which is atelectasis. These actions do not primarily prevent bleeding, sinusitis, or asthma.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: The nurse is caring for a client with chronic respiratory failure. What are the signs and symptoms of chronic respiratory failure?
options: Progressive loss of lung function with history of normal lung function
Sudden loss of lung function with history of normal lung function
Sudden loss of lung function associated with chronic disease
Progressive loss of lung function associated with chronic disease
correctAnswers: Progressive loss of lung function associated with chronic disease
rationale: Chronic respiratory failure develops as a progressive loss of lung function associated with chronic disease. Sudden loss of function suggests acute respiratory failure rather than chronic respiratory failure.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-05-respiratory-pathophysiology.md
stem: The volume of air inhaled and exhaled with each breath is termed:
rationale: Tidal volume is the amount of air inhaled and exhaled with each normal breath. Vital capacity, residual volume, and expiratory reserve volume describe different lung-volume measurements.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: A backflow of blood is noted in the left atria from the left ventricle. The client is suffering from a defect in which valve?
rationale: The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle. Backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium indicates mitral regurgitation, not a defect in the tricuspid, pulmonic, or aortic valve.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: A nurse is caring for a client with hypertension. If blood pressure is not adequately controlled, what organs can be damaged? (Select all that apply.)
rationale: Uncontrolled hypertension damages high-flow target organs, especially the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes. The pancreas and gallbladder are not the classic target organs emphasized for hypertensive end-organ damage.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: When teaching about safe disposal of prescription medications at home, the nurse should include which instructions? (Select all that apply)
options: Scratch out or mark personal information on prescription containers.
Give the medication to a family member, in case they need it.
Mix unused medications with undesirable substances before putting them in the trash.
Flush medications only if the label specifically instructs it is safe.
Always place medications in impermeable, nondescript containers before discarding.
correctAnswers: Scratch out or mark personal information on prescription containers.
Mix unused medications with undesirable substances before putting them in the trash.
Flush medications only if the label specifically instructs it is safe.
Always place medications in impermeable, nondescript containers before discarding.
rationale: Safe medication disposal includes removing personal information, mixing many unused drugs with undesirable substances before trash disposal, using a sealed nondescript container, and flushing only when the label specifically says to. Sharing prescription medication with family is unsafe.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: The nurse is assessing a new client who states being allergic to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs). What subsequent assessment should the nurse prioritize?
options: asking the client what the client's response is to taking NSAIDs
assessing the client for signs and symptoms of inflammation
assessing the client's pain tolerance and expectations for pain control
asking if the client has tolerated opioids and acetaminophen in the past
correctAnswers: asking the client what the client's response is to taking NSAIDs
rationale: The nurse should clarify what reaction the client has with NSAIDs because “allergy” may mean anything from GI upset to anaphylaxis. Knowing the actual response guides safe medication selection more than immediately focusing on pain tolerance or inflammation.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: A client presents to the emergency department via ambulance with a heart rate of 130 beats/minute and a sawtooth waveform pattern per cardiac monitor. The nurse is most correct to alert the medical team of the presence of a client with which disorder?
rationale: A sawtooth waveform pattern with a rapid rhythm is characteristic of atrial flutter. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular, ventricular tachycardia is a ventricular wide-complex rhythm, and PVCs are isolated premature beats.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: Dihydropyridine type of calcium-channel blockers primarily act on blood vessels, so they have less negative inotropic effect on the heart. Nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, havine greater effects on the heart rate and contractility, and some cardiac tachyarrhythmias.
rationale: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers act mainly on vascular smooth muscle, so they have less direct negative inotropic effect. Nondihydropyridines have stronger cardiac effects on rate and contractility and can be used for some tachyarrhythmias.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: The nurse is caring for a client who returns to the clinic 3 months after starting a new prescription for metoprolol 50 mg by mouth daily. The client reports they have been exercising and assessing their blood pressure daily. The client states they discontinued the metoprolol 2 days ago since blood pressure measurements have been between 110/60 mm Hg and 128/72 mm Hg since the last clinic visit. What response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "We will get laboratory data today, and this will tell us if we can stop the medication."
"Let's consult the doctor since your vital signs may indicate that you no longer need this medication."
"Discontinuing this medication suddenly can cause blood pressure and heart rate problems."
correctAnswers: "Discontinuing this medication suddenly can cause blood pressure and heart rate problems."
rationale: Beta blockers should not be stopped abruptly because rebound sympathetic effects can worsen blood pressure, heart rate, or ischemic symptoms. Normal home blood pressure readings should be discussed with the provider rather than prompting sudden discontinuation.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: The nurse is preparing to administer a prescribed drug to a client with a history of renal disease. Why should the nurse anticipate administering a lower dose than for a client with healthy kidneys?
options: Absorption will be increased because of fluid accumulation.
Excretion is likely to take place slowly.
The client likely has impaired drug metabolism.
Distribution will be delayed, increasing the risk of adverse effects.
correctAnswers: Excretion is likely to take place slowly.
rationale: Renal disease can slow drug excretion, allowing medication to accumulate and increasing adverse-effect risk. A lower dose may be needed because clearance is reduced, not because absorption is increased or metabolism is necessarily impaired.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: A client is receiving 250 mg of a drug that has a half-life of 12 hours. How much drug would remain after 36 hours?
rationale: A 12-hour half-life means the amount halves every 12 hours. After 36 hours, three half-lives have passed: 250 mg to 125 mg, then 63 mg, then about 31 mg remains.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: A client with chronic pain is upset because their prescription for hydrocodone has no refills. Which information will the nurse include in response to the client?
options: "The medication you are on is being tested for medical use and is restricted.”
“There is a shortage of medications to treat your condition.”
"Hydrocodone is a Schedule II medication that has the potential for misuse."
"The federal government regulates all medications used to treat your condition."
correctAnswers: "Hydrocodone is a Schedule II medication that has the potential for misuse."
rationale: Hydrocodone is a Schedule II controlled substance with accepted medical use but significant misuse and dependence potential. Schedule II medications generally cannot be refilled in the same way as many noncontrolled prescriptions.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: A patient is having trouble swallowing. The provider has prescribed a drug in the form of large capsules; however, the nurse checks whether the drug is available in liquid form. The nurse is establishing the right:
rationale: Checking whether a large capsule can be replaced by a liquid form is about the right route and formulation for safe administration. The dose, time, and drug identity may be correct, but the route/form must fit the patient’s ability to swallow.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: A nurse has been administering a drug to a client intramuscularly (IM). The health care provider discontinued the IM dose and wrote an order for the drug to be given orally. The nurse notices that the oral dosage is considerably higher than the parenteral dose and understands that this due to:
rationale: Oral drugs may undergo first-pass metabolism in the liver before reaching systemic circulation, reducing bioavailability. A higher oral dose may therefore be needed compared with an IM or IV dose.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: When explaining the types of leukocytes produced by the bone marrow, the nurse describes lymphocytes. Which would the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
rationale: Lymphocytes include B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells. Neutrophils, basophils, and monocytes are leukocytes too, but they are not lymphocytes in this classification.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: A client has developed a wound infection and leukocytes are leaving the bloodstream to perform phagocytosis on pathogens. What white cells are most likely performing this function?
rationale: Neutrophils are the primary early phagocytes that leave the bloodstream during acute bacterial infection. Monocytes can become macrophages later, while basophils and eosinophils have different immune roles.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: Which adverse effect is most associated with long-term monoclonal antibody use?
options: Increased risk of infection and malignancy
correctAnswers: Increased risk of infection and malignancy
rationale: Many monoclonal antibodies suppress specific immune pathways, so long-term use can increase infection risk and may increase malignancy risk. Hypertension or constipation can occur with some drugs, but infection and malignancy are the broad class concern emphasized here.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: Six months after undergoing transplantation, a client asks the health care provider if it would be all right for them to volunteer at the local children’s health clinic. The client has limited adverse effects from the immunosuppressant drugs and is beginning to feel healthy again. The health care provider suggests alternate volunteer options because:
options: It will increase the risk of rejection.
It is too soon to volunteer in a clinic setting.
The client may develop an infectious process at the clinic.
The client may not have the stamina to work at the clinic.
correctAnswers: The client may develop an infectious process at the clinic.
rationale: Immunosuppressant therapy lowers immune defenses after transplant, increasing vulnerability to infectious exposures. A children’s health clinic may expose the client to contagious illnesses, so infection risk is the reason to suggest alternate volunteer options.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: Which medication(s) are examples of T- and B-cell suppressors? (Select all that apply.)
rationale: Tacrolimus, prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, and methotrexate all suppress immune-cell activity through different mechanisms. They are used to reduce immune responses in conditions such as transplant rejection prevention or autoimmune disease.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: As the nurse, you identify MC has modfiable and non-modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease. What modifiable risk factor do you identify when taking her history?
options: MC is a person with rheumatoid arthritis
Biological parent had a heart attack at 58 years of age
rationale: Current smoking is modifiable because the patient can reduce or stop tobacco exposure. Age, sex assigned at birth, inflammatory disease history, and family history are important risk factors but are not modifiable in the same way.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: MC's provider recommended smoking cessation today and for her to start taking lisinopril for her blood pressure. She is to continue taking her rheumatoid arthritis medication. As the nurse, you know lisinopril is an ___ , and methotrexate is a ___
rationale: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor used for blood pressure control, while methotrexate is an antimetabolite immunosuppressive disease-modifying antirheumatic drug. The distinction matters because their therapeutic targets and major safety teaching points differ.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: You understand that lisinopril's mechanism of action.....
options: prevents the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II in the lungs, which is a potent vasoconstrictor
blocks the flood of calcium ions across cardiac muscle during depolarization
prevents renin from being converted to angiotensin I, which is a potent vasodilator
blocks beta-adrenergic receptors, which decreases the sympathetic nervous response
correctAnswers: prevents the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II in the lungs, which is a potent vasoconstrictor
rationale: Lisinopril inhibits ACE, reducing conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Less angiotensin II means less vasoconstriction and less aldosterone-mediated sodium/water retention, which lowers blood pressure.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-06-cardiovascular-pharm-immunology-hidden-key.md
stem: What patient education should you provide to MC about taking lisinopril? (Select all that apply)
options: You should lower your salt intake as it impacts your blood pressure and instead use potassium chloride salt substitute to flavor food
Take the medication at the same time of day
If you develop swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat, or develop trouble breathing, call 911. You may be experiencing angioedema, a rare side effect of ACE inhibitors
You may notice a non-productive cough, which is a common side effect. If this happens, please contact our office.
correctAnswers: Take the medication at the same time of day
If you develop swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat, or develop trouble breathing, call 911. You may be experiencing angioedema, a rare side effect of ACE inhibitors
You may notice a non-productive cough, which is a common side effect. If this happens, please contact our office.
rationale: ACE inhibitor teaching should include taking the medication consistently, reporting persistent dry cough, and seeking emergency care for facial, tongue, throat swelling, or breathing trouble because of angioedema risk. Potassium salt substitutes should be avoided unless approved because ACE inhibitors can raise potassium.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
stem: The nurse is performing a history for a client who is concerned about developing coronary artery disease since it "runs in the family." What modifiable risk factor does the nurse identify when taking the history?
options: Biological parent had a myocardial infarction at age 42
rationale: Current smoking is modifiable because the patient can reduce or stop tobacco exposure. Age, sex assigned at birth, inflammatory disease history, and family history are important risk factors but are not modifiable in the same way.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
stem: The critical care nurse is caring for a client with bradycardia after cardiovascular surgery. The nurse knows that the heart rate is determined by myocardial cells with the fastest depolarizing rate. Under normal circumstances, where are these cells located?
rationale: Under normal circumstances, the SA node has the fastest spontaneous depolarization rate and sets the heart’s rhythm. The AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje fibers can pace more slowly if needed but are not the normal primary pacemaker.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
stem: Which New York Heart Association classification of heart failure has a poor prognosis and includes symptoms of cardiac insufficiency at rest?
rationale: NYHA class IV heart failure includes symptoms at rest and has the poorest prognosis among the listed classes. Classes I through III involve no symptoms or symptoms with increasing levels of activity rather than at rest.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
stem: The nurse is assessing the client for left-sided heart failure. Which symptom would the nurse identify as left-ventricular heart failure? (Select all that apply.)
rationale: Left-sided heart failure backs blood into the pulmonary circulation and also reduces forward cardiac output. Cough and dyspnea reflect pulmonary congestion, and tachycardia is a compensatory response; neck vein distention and hepatic engorgement fit right-sided systemic venous congestion better.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
stem: A backflow of blood is noted in the left atria from the left ventricle. The client is suffering from a defect in which valve?
rationale: The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle. Backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium indicates mitral regurgitation, not a defect in the tricuspid, pulmonic, or aortic valve.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
stem: A nurse is educating a group of nursing students about the heart's chambers and the muscular septum wall. What information by a nursing student demonstrates a correct understanding about the four chambers into which the heart is divided? (Select all that apply.)
options: The interior of the heart is divided into two chambers.
Ventricles are high-pressure chambers because they pump blood out of the heart.
The thin-walled, low-pressure chambers are the receiving centers for blood.
The left ventricle is the thickest chamber and it pumps blood to the rest of the body.
correctAnswers: Ventricles are high-pressure chambers because they pump blood out of the heart.
The thin-walled, low-pressure chambers are the receiving centers for blood.
The left ventricle is the thickest chamber and it pumps blood to the rest of the body.
rationale: The atria are thin-walled receiving chambers, while the ventricles are higher-pressure pumping chambers. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood systemically; the heart has four chambers, not two.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
stem: A student asks the instructor what the goal of drug therapy is in cardiogenic shock. What is the most appropriate response from the instructor?
options: Restore and maintain adequate tissue perfusion
Replace fluids the client has lost
correctAnswers: Restore and maintain adequate tissue perfusion
rationale: The goal in cardiogenic shock is to restore and maintain adequate tissue perfusion despite pump failure. Simply increasing heart rate or replacing fluid is not always appropriate and does not capture the overall treatment goal.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
stem: Which symptoms would likely be present in a client with right-ventricular heart failure? (Select all that apply)
rationale: Right-sided heart failure causes systemic venous congestion, leading to peripheral edema, neck vein distention, hepatic congestion, and nocturia. Orthopnea, crackles, and frothy sputum are more typical of left-sided pulmonary congestion.

source: Saved course quiz/test capture: 2026-05-13-quiz-07-cardiovascular-pathophysiology-hidden-key.md
